subject: ba
title: Business Survival and Failure in Nigeria
objectives: Identify the macro and micro challenges facing Nigerian businesses.
Distinguish business survival from business success, and analyse the causes of business failure.
Recognise the indicators and symptoms of impending business failure.
Formulate remedies and survival strategies suited to the Nigerian business environment.
study:
Nigeria offers a genuinely large market, but a uniquely difficult operating terrain — in 2019 it ranked 131st of 190 countries in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business Report, and roughly 80% of new businesses fail within their first three years.

Key termBusiness Survival — meeting obligations and likely turning a profit, without necessarily positioning for long-term prosperity. Business Success goes further: doing this while actively preparing for a prosperous future.

The specific pressures Nigerian businesses face include: limited access to capital (only about 6% of Nigerian SMEs have formal credit access, per the CBN); inadequate infrastructure (Nigeria loses an estimated 2–3% of GDP annually to unreliable power, per the African Development Bank); inconsistent regulation (business is governed principally by CAMA 2020, but policy shifts often); corruption and bureaucratic red tape; naira volatility complicating dollar-denominated trade; and a lack of market information — 66% of Nigerian business owners cite difficulty finding new customers for exactly this reason.

Exam tipRemember the specific statistics — 131st ranking, 6% SME credit access, 2–3% GDP lost to power problems, 66% citing poor market information. These exact figures show up directly in exam questions.

A U.S. Small Business Administration study found that roughly 66% of new businesses survive 2+ years, but only 50% survive 4+ years. Requirements for survival include adequate capital, a living business plan under constant review, genuinely knowing the market (not assuming), adequate control mechanisms, and monitoring competitors, technology, policy and customer behaviour.

Business failure is a company's inability to meet its financial obligations, forcing it to shut down or suspend operations. Causes split into Financial (inadequate working capital, poor accounting records) and Non-Financial causes — including growing too fast, which risks losing control and overstretching the business's resources. Failures themselves come in three flavours: Preventable/Predictable failures (the most damaging, usually from a startup's failure to follow best practice), Unavoidable failures (natural disasters, pandemics, recessions), and Intelligent/Intellectual failures (experimenting with new ideas — delivering valuable learning cheaply, common in tech).

Warning signs to watch for include deteriorating working capital (insufficient cash for day-to-day obligations), a high debt ratio, declining sales and profit, and declining capacity utilisation (which raises per-unit costs as economies of scale are lost). Remedies include government intervention (sound monetary/fiscal policy, better infrastructure), management acquiring real financial knowledge, careful market analysis, and avoiding over-trading — specialising in genuine areas of competence rather than being a jack of all trades.
recap:
• Nigeria-specific pressures: limited credit access (6% of SMEs), power losses (2–3% of GDP), CAMA 2020 regulation, naira volatility, poor market information (66% of owners affected).
  • Business survival ≠ business success: survival = meeting obligations profitably; success = also positioning for long-term prosperity.
  • Business failure causes: Financial (working capital, accounting) vs Non-Financial (e.g. growing too fast).
  • Failure types: Preventable/Predictable (most damaging) · Unavoidable (external shocks) · Intelligent/Intellectual (cheap learning from experimentation).
  • Warning signs: deteriorating working capital, high debt ratio, declining sales/profit/capacity utilisation.
  • Remedies: government intervention, sound financial knowledge, market analysis, avoiding over-trading.

quiz.q: Business failure is best described as:
opts: A company's inability to meet its financial obligations, forcing it to shut down or suspend operations
A guaranteed permanent state for all new companies
A synonym for record company profit
A situation that only affects government agencies

quiz.q: Causes of business failure are broadly grouped into Financial Causes and:
opts: Weather-Related Causes only
International Causes only
Religious Causes only
Non-Financial Causes

quiz.q: Which of the following is a Financial cause of business failure?
opts: Overwhelming market demand
Too much available skilled labour
Inadequate working capital and poor accounting record keeping
Excessive customer loyalty

quiz.q: 'Growing too fast' as a cause of business failure primarily risks:
opts: Automatic increase in product quality
Loss of control and overstretching of the business's resources and financial base
Complete elimination of all competition
Guaranteed permanent success with no downside

quiz.q: According to Wallstreetmojo.com, Preventable (Predictable) Business Failures are considered:
opts: The most damaging type of failure, often from a startup's inability to follow best practices
Only relevant to large multinational corporations
Impossible to occur under any circumstances
The least damaging and most easily ignored type of failure

quiz.q: Unavoidable Business Failures are typically caused by:
opts: Deliberate poor planning by management alone
Unpredictable events such as natural disasters, pandemics, wars and recessions
Overly cautious business strategies
Excessive customer satisfaction

quiz.q: Intelligent (Intellectual) Business Failures arise primarily from:
opts: Complete refusal to ever try anything new
Guaranteed immediate profitability with no risk
Experimenting with new products or strategies, delivering valuable learning at relatively low cost
Government-imposed shutdowns only

quiz.q: The example of Friska (a UK restaurant chain) closing in 2021 illustrates business failure due to:
opts: A currency devaluation crisis
Excessive employee turnover
A shortage of raw materials only
The COVID-19 pandemic and associated lockdown restrictions

quiz.q: 'Deterioration of Working Capital', as a symptom of business failure, refers to:
opts: An excessive surplus of cash with no productive use
Guaranteed increasing sales figures
Insufficient cash to meet the day-to-day financial obligations of the company
Improved product quality relative to competitors

quiz.q: 'Declining Capacity Utilisation', as a symptom of business failure, tends to result in:
opts: Decreased cost per unit of production automatically
Increased cost per unit of production, as economies of scale are lost
No impact whatsoever on production costs
Guaranteed increase in market share

quiz.q: As a remedy/survival strategy, 'Avoidance of Over-Trading' suggests that management should:
opts: Attempt to enter every possible business sector simultaneously
Ignore their own areas of competence entirely
Specialise in areas of business where they have sound competence, rather than being a 'jack of all trades'
Avoid any form of specialisation whatsoever

quiz.q: Government Intervention, as a remedy for business failure, primarily involves:
opts: Removing all business regulations with no oversight at all
Guaranteeing profit for every business regardless of performance
Complete elimination of all private enterprise
Conducive monetary/fiscal policy and provision of better infrastructural facilities
